newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH CABINET HUNTS FUNDS FOR FLOOD RELIEF.
newsitem.headline: POLISH CABINET HUNTS FUNDS FOR FLOOD RELIEF.

text.p: Floods ebbing from hundreds of shattered communities hit new areas of Poland on Tuesday as the government sought ways to fund relief fast without further harming the economy or its own re-election hopes.

Waters retreated in hard-hit parts of the south to reveal smashed homes, broken bridges and torn roads covered in filth, but officials estimated that 2,200 sq kms remained flooded, included much of the cities of Wroclaw and Opole.
Communities downstrean along the Odra fearfully braced for a huge surge of high water rolling mercilessly northward down the river towards the German border and the sea.
Resident of the town of Glogow, warned by televised images of horrors further south, took no chances as water seeped in.
"People are evacuating themselves. After the experience of people in the south, they are taking their things and going," said central crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes.
The region's worst natural disaster in centuries, caused by downpours last week, has killed at least 38 people in Poland and also brought death and destruction to its Czech neighbours.
Poland's coalition cabinet met to agree proposed changes to the 1997 budget and dozens of laws that will be put to an special parliament session on Wednesday to ease relief effort.
Government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska told a news conference that at least 60,000 households had been hit and would qualify for quick $600 payouts to provide essentials.
"We are talking about at least 50-60,000 families and this figure will grow as time passes," she said.

Ex-communist Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz last week ruled out changing the budget to find extra funds. But as the vast scale of the disaster became clear and the opposition flung charges of incompetence, he changed his mind.

The premier's Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), the dominant coalition party, is fighting an opposition alliance led by the Solidarity union in September 21 elections and analysts say its actions now could mean victory or defeat.
Warsaw region's Solidarity chief Maciej Jankowski was scathing about official performance during the crisis.
"In any normal democracy, there would be a vote of no confidence in the government after actions like these," PAP news agency quoted Jankowski as saying on Tuesday.
Cimoszewicz told reporters he would ask parliament to borrow up to an extra 2.5 billion zlotys ($740 million) from the central bank this year to ensure it had enough cash.

Worries over Poland's deficit and inflation helped send the zloty rate down by five percent against a basket of currencies on Tuesday and Cimoszewicz tried to calm any jitters over such possible heavy borrowing.
"The increase of the borrowing limit is to ensure temporary financing. It is not an additional 2.5 billion zlotys in the economy," Cimoszewicz said in a break in the cabinet session.

The government will also seek an increase in foreign borrowing limits to allow a $300 million World Bank loan. It rejected however as not immediately necessary a controversial idea of a universal flood tax.

Largely by yanking money from other budget goals and halting capital projects the government has already lined up 650 million zlotys for flood relief and the prime minister said this would be enough for now.
Cimoszewicz earlier rejected opposition criticisms that the government had so far done too little, too late, saying the heaviness of the floods was totally unexpected.
"I think any casual opinions about lack of action, lack of preparation...is not necessarily the truth," he said.
The premier told public radio that any praise or blame should come later and the main task was to rebuild as much as possible in the next four or five months before winter.
